docs.title: Dams, missile bases and water
docs.text:
A statistical assessment of a New York Times claim about Iranian dams

Omid S. Solari, Ph.D. (Ph.D. in Statistics, University of California, Berkeley)

On 16 November 2026 The New York Times suggested that Iran's dams overlap geographically with the underground missile sites struck by the United States and Israel, that Iran has an unusually large number of dams, and that the dams may have been built to supply those sites. This site documents an open, reproducible test of each element of that argument.

The data do not support the claim. Missile bases are not unusually close to dams, military bases near water are the norm worldwide, and Iran's dam numbers are not unusual for a water-scarce country.

Read the full report (PDF) Source code on GitHub

docs.title: Findings
docs.text: Claim in the article What the data show Dams and missile sites overlap Rejected. Not significant against random locations in Iran (median 48.1 km, p = 0.146); after matching on terrain, towns and rivers the bases lie farther from dams than expected (p = 0.908). The mean is shorter than random (p = 0.011) but not after matching. The overlap is distinctive to military sites Rejected. Towns and airports show the same apparent overlap; it reflects settlement geography. Military siting near water is anomalous Rejected. Iran's launch bases rank 49th of 54 states for proximity to the nearest dam or coast; military sites in 91% of states lie closer to water. Relative to each state's own geography: 29th for dams, 47th for dams or coast. Iran has unusually many dams Rejected. Dam density of 3.3 per 10,000 km², below Spain (25.1), Turkey (11.9) and Morocco (6.7); construction peaks in 2015–2019, the same period as Turkey.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text: The article's full text, Nima Shokri's map of 533 dams and the article's strike map are not public. Global Dam Watch (183 Iranian dams) and the Alma Research Center's list of 25 launch bases are used instead. See Data sources and the limitations section of the report.

docs.title: Co-location test
docs.text:
For each of the 25 launch bases, the great-circle distance to the nearest dam is computed. The 25 distances are summarised by their median (primary statistic), their mean and the share within 20 km. Each statistic is compared with 10,000 draws from a sequence of null models of increasing stringency:

Null Comparison sites CSR Uniformly random locations in Iran (cells weighted by area). The comparison implicit in a visual reading of two maps. M1 For each base, a random location among the 40 grid cells closest to it in elevation and local relief. M2 As M1, additionally matched on distance to the nearest town of at least 50,000. M3 As M2, additionally matched on distance to the nearest mapped river. RIV Bases fixed; the dams are relocated at random along Iran's river network.

Matching is nearest-neighbour in standardised covariate space on a 10 arc-minute grid; sampled locations are jittered uniformly within their cell. All p-values are one-sided and test whether the bases are closer to dams than expected. Placebo point sets (towns, airports) are run through the same CSR and M3 tests. Sensitivity is assessed across match sizes k = 20, 40, 80 and three statistics.

docs.title: Global comparison
docs.text: All current military sites in Wikidata with coordinates (instances of military base, Q245016, or any subclass, excluding police barracks and dissolved sites) are assigned to states by point-in-polygon. For each site the distance to the nearest dam (Global Dam Watch) and to the sea coast (Natural Earth 1:10m) is computed. States with at least 15 sites are ranked by median and mean distance with 95% bootstrap intervals; dependent territories are excluded. The ratio of the median distance for military sites to the median for 2,000 random points in the same state controls for each state's geography and for country-specific gaps in dam coverage.

docs.title: Dam construction
docs.text: Dam densities use national counts; construction timelines use Global Dam Watch completion years.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:osolari/iran-dams-colocation.git
cd iran-dams-colocation
pip install -r requirements.txt
bash src/fetch_data.sh   # optional: refresh public inputs (Global Dam Watch must be fetched manually)
./run_all.sh             # data preparation, analyses, figures, LaTeX tables, report PDF, site pages

The random seed is fixed (SEED = 20261116 in src/common.py); a full run takes about two minutes.

docs.title: Documentation site
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements-docs.txt   # MkDocs pinned below 2.0
mkdocs serve        # local preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs gh-deploy    # build and push to the gh-pages branch

The GitHub Actions workflow in .github/workflows/docs.yml rebuilds and publishes the site on every push to main.

docs.title: Robustness
docs.text:
• Large dams only (66): CSR p = 0.131; M3 p = 0.725.
  • Struck in June 2025 against not attacked: medians 48.1 and 56.9 km, Mann–Whitney p = 0.30.
  • Sensitivity to statistic and match size: results/tables/iran_sensitivity.csv.

docs.title: Not available to this analysis
docs.text:
• The NYT article text (nytimes.com is blocked to the analysis tools; syndicated excerpts used instead).
  • Nima Shokri's map of 533 Iranian dams (unpublished).
  • The NYT's map of 2026 strikes on suspected missile sites (unpublished).
  • OpenStreetMap military features via Overpass (host not reachable at run time); Wikidata used instead.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Alma lists one base as "Ahbar (ابهر)"; the Persian name is Abhar, used here.
  • GDW is the full global shapefile (239 MB unzipped) and is not committed. Download GDW_v1_0_shp.zip from figshare and unzip into data/external/ to rebuild from scratch; otherwise prepare.py uses the committed processed CSV.
